intro: Rachmaninoff wrote Polichinelle, Op. 3 No. 4 (Allegro vivace), at nineteen; it alternates loud, heavy notes with soft, rapid flurries and has a song-like middle section. The composer plays it in this 1923 recording.

sections.label: A · Notes at fff, grace-note figures at ppp
sections.mNote: Allegro vivace; fff notes alternate with ppp grace-note figures.

sections.label: B · Agitato, melody within running notes
sections.mNote: An accented melody runs over long bass notes.

sections.label: A′ · Return of the opening theme
sections.mNote: Grace notes return, played quietly, before the final detached chords.

cues.title: Opening, fff and ppp contrasts
cues.text: Two notes are marked fff, followed by a rapid figure at ppp. The hands jump between these extremes, and grace notes and rests break up the line. Both hands soon play full chords at ff.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 1: Allegro vivace, fff single notes, ppp grace-note figures and ff chords. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/morceaux-de-fantaisie/polichinelle-op-3-4.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Title suggested by Slonov, 1892
cues.text: In 1892 the tenor Mikhail Slonov suggested the title Polichinelle to his friend Rachmaninoff, who was assembling pieces around his C♯ minor Prelude for a concert in Kharkov. Gutheil published the five Morceaux de fantaisie the following February, dedicated to Anton Arensky.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s notes for Hyperion CDA66081 give Slonov’s suggestion, the Kharkov concert, February 1893 publication and dedication to Arensky. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: Victor recordings, 1920 and 1923
cues.text: Rachmaninoff first recorded Polichinelle for Victor on 20 October 1920, at the company’s laboratory in Camden, New Jersey, and that take was destroyed. He recorded it again in New York on 6 March 1923. This second take was issued on Victor 74807, and on 6452 with Chopin’s F♯ major Nocturne.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix C-24643 lists take 1 (20 October 1920, Camden, Church Building Laboratory, destroyed) and take 2 (6 March 1923, New York, master), issued on Victor 74807 and 6452: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700009866/C-24643-Polichinelle_op._3_no._4. Victor 6452 couples it with the Nocturne in F♯ major: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/41140

cues.title: Agitato section
cues.text: At Agitato a long slurred line moves over held bass notes. Accents mark out a melody within the fast figures. Each group of semiquavers and triplets above it is slurred.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 4, from Agitato: slurred semiquavers and triplets with accented lower melody and long bass notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening figures
cues.text: Heavy chords interrupt the running figures. The grace notes of the opening then return at ppp, placed between short, accented notes. The smooth middle section has ended, and the hands jump again.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 6: sfff chords followed by the return of the ppp grace-note figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing chords
cues.text: The closing chords are short and detached, marked fff, with rests between them. The last fermata is placed over the final rest.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 8, final system: fff detached chords and a fermata over the final rest.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Descent into the Agitato
transitions.from: A · Notes at fff, grace-note figures at ppp
transitions.to: B · Agitato, melody within running notes
transitions.how: The quick figures descend into the bass, with rests in the left hand. At Agitato, a new phrase begins over a low octave. Slurred right-hand figures carry an accented melody over bass notes held for a whole bar. Above the bass, semiquavers alternate with triplets.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 4, second and third systems: descending figures, rests and Agitato over whole-note basses.

transitions.title: Heavy chords, then the quiet flurry
transitions.from: B · Agitato, melody within running notes
transitions.to: A′ · Return of the opening theme
transitions.how: The left hand strikes chords marked sfff, each cut short by rests, while the right hand continues its running figures. Further pairs of chords break into the descent. Both hands then drop to ppp, and the grace-note figures of the opening return with the same sudden leaps across the keyboard.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 6: interrupted sfff chords and the return of the ppp grace-note passage.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano, performed by the composer
fields.note: No performing score edition is identified, and the printed text is not asserted to match the performance.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: DAHR’s approved take 2 is dated 6 March 1923; the Archive filename and the RCA register give the same date. Take 1 of 20 October 1920 was destroyed.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for the approved take; the 1920 take was made in Camden, New Jersey.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Victor is the original label; the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Victor 74807 (12-inch single-faced) and Victor 6452 (12-inch double-faced, with Chopin’s Nocturne in F♯ major); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: DAHR names the matrix, takes and issues. The link between that take and this digital file rests on the RCA register (which names the matrix and take for the CD track) and the uploader’s CD identification; no waveform or run-out comparison with the disc was made.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 6452, recorded 1923).
fields.note: DAHR’s catalogue record for Victor 6452 gives a publication date of [1923], a catalogue-derived year rather than a release day. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists “In F Sharp Major (Op. 15, No. 2) and Polichinelle — Piano — Rachmaninoff”, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
